"Sorry, we thought we had a concrete case against you...but it turns out you were really innocent. Sorry about frying your balls/ovaries and any hope you may ever have of starting a family./Sorry about killing you and ending your life, even though you claimed to the moment we threw the switch to electrocute you that you were innocent. What can we do to make it better for you?" Suddenly doesn't sound so good when you consider it coming from the government official that mandated those things be done to you, does it? In short, because the risks of irreversible damage, and society's risk of being complicit with wronging such an individual, forces me to oppose such a policy. Plus, several modern societies tried chemical castration for sexual deviants in the past, and it turned out to be a horrific policy. Chem Castration would be a step backwards, in the worst sense of the term. Look up the case of Alan Turing, the father of modern computing, for more info.

2) Efficiency of Policy - The point of incarceration is to remove a threat to the public from the populace. Once you have incarcerated a violent offender, you have performed that necessary task, for however long you have sentenced them. In your suggested case, if they are violent enough that you can justify chemically castrating them, then I think it's also safe to say that you would be fine with giving them a permanent sentence behind bars without parole. If we were to solve the idiocy that has been substance prohibition, this policy would be child's play to enact, and we would have more than enough room for society's violent offenders, seeing as violent crimes, until recently with the rise of BLM, have been bottoming out over the years. This would also save the issue of the irreversible damage done by shriveling up someone's balls or ovaries, and then finding out years down the line you irreversibly fried the reproductive system of an innocent person. This, however, speaks more to a problem of what we currently punish with incarceration, and calls more for a reform of general criminal law, than it does Sex Offender criminal law, specifically.

3) Effect of Policy On Potential Victims - Chemical castration only kills the sex drive. It does not kill the drive to prey on others. Crimes like child molestation are often more about the power exerted over and dominating a helpless subject, than it is about the sex. Sure, you would reduce some small amount of this crime, but I suspect the vast majority, specifically the Crimes-of-Power contingent, would continue. Even worse, now the guy can't get it up to rape the kid? He's going to be even more frustrated and brutal, now...so he's going to likely reach for something even more sadistic, like a broomstick or a blade. As a result, chemical castration as an alternative to incarceration is a horrible idea. And if you're not talking about as an alternative to incarceration, then you're just stacking additional punishment on top of a sentence that already achieves the primary objectives by removing the violent threat from the populace.

In short, there's nothing to be additionally gained from this policy, and quite a bit to lose, especially in comparison to what our current options are.
